results.title: Hyperedge Modeling in Hypergraph Neural Networks by ...
results.content: Hyperedge Modeling in Hypergraph Neural Networks by using Densest Overlapping Subgraphs Mehrad Soltani University of Windsor Windsor, Canada soltani8@uwindsor.ca Luis Rueda University of Windsor Windsor, Canada lrueda@uwindsor.ca Abstract—Hypergraphs tackle the limitations of traditional graphs by introducing hyperedges. In this paper, we propose a solution to the DOS problem via Agglomerative Greedy Enu-meration (DOSAGE) algorithm as a novel approach to enhance the process of generating the densest overlapping subgraphs and, hence, a robust construction of the hypergraphs. Index Terms—hypergraphs, hypergraph neural networks, hy-peredge generation, overlapping densest subgraphs, graph rep-resentation learning I. The main contributions of this paper are summarized as follows: (i) enhance HGNN accuracy with a new hypergraph modeling method based on the densest overlapping subgraphs; (ii) design a new algorithm for finding the densest overlapping subgraphs; (iii) define a new problem: the constrained overlapping subgraphs with full coverage, arXiv:2409.10340v1 [cs.LG] 16 Sep 2024 specific subgraph size, and diameter. V. METHODOLOGY Our DOSAGE algorithm creates hyperedges based on the overlapping densest subgraphs in a graph based on three parameters that are K, which is the total number of sub-graphs and hence a number of hyperedges, the minimum and maximum size that is the minimum and maximum number of vertices in one hyperedge. We take the input graph G = (V, E′) from the 3-Clique Partition problem and use it as the input graph for the constrained Top-k-Overlapping Densest Subgraphs problem. We take the solution W from the constrained Top-k-Overlapping Densest Subgraphs problem and use the sub-graphs G[S1], G[S2], and G[S3] to construct three cliques V1, V2, and V3 in the original graph G = (V, E′). Constrained Top-k-Overlapping Densest Subgraphs (CTODS): Given: A graph Gh = (V, E), positive integers k, α, β, and a real number r. The results from both datasets indicate that the DOSAGE algorithm’s hypergraph construction method, based on the densest overlapping subgraphs, offers superior performance in node classification tasks compared to existing GNN and HGNN models. Unlike traditional graph neural networks (GNNs) and existing hypergraph neural networks (HGNNs), DOSAGE focuses on capturing complex relationships within data by constructing hyperedges that reflect more intricate and overlapping struc-tures.

results.title: Graph Theory - Hypergraphs
results.content: * Graph Theory - k-Connected Graphs. * Graph Theory - 2-Vertex-Connected Graphs. * Graph Theory - 2-Edge-Connected Graphs. * Graph Theory - Connectivity in Planar Graphs. * Graph Theory - A\* Search Algorithm. # Graph Theory - Hypergraphs. ## Hypergraphs in Graph Theory. A **hypergraph** is a generalization of a graph in which an edge, known as a **hyperedge**, can connect any number of vertices. Unlike standard edges in a traditional graph, which connect exactly two vertices, hyperedges in hypergraphs can connect more than two vertices. Unlike regular edges in a graph, which only connect two vertices, a hyperedge can connect any number of vertices, ranging from two to the entire set of vertices in the hypergraph. A **simple hypergraph** is a hypergraph where each hyperedge contains no repeated vertices. Simple hypergraphs are often studied in combinatorics and graph theory. A **multi-hypergraph** allows repeated vertices in a hyperedge. A **uniform hypergraph** is a type of hypergraph where every edge (or hyperedge) connects the same number of vertices. A **non-uniform hypergraph** is a type of hypergraph where the edges (or hyperedges) can connect different numbers of vertices. Unlike uniform hypergraphs, where every edge connects the same number of vertices, non-uniform hypergraphs allow hyperedges of varying sizes, meaning some edges may connect two vertices, others may connect three, and so on. In traditional graphs, adjacency refers to the relationship between two vertices that are connected by an edge. Similarly, two vertices are said to be adjacent in the hypergraph if they appear together in at least one hyperedge. The degree of a vertex can be different from its degree in a regular graph because a hyperedge can involve multiple vertices. A hypergraph is said to be **vertex-connected** if there is a path between any two vertices that passes through a series of hyperedges. Similarly, a hypergraph is **edge-connected** if there is a way to traverse between any two hyperedges through a sequence of vertices. A hypergraph is a type of graph where edges, called hyperedges, can connect more than two vertices. Centrality measures in hypergraphs work similarly to those in regular graphs, but they consider the more complex relationships between multiple vertices at once.

View a PDF of the paper titled Hyperedge Anomaly Detection with Hypergraph Neural Network, by Md. Tanvir Alam and 2 other authors. > Abstract:Hypergraph is a data structure that enables us to model higher-order associations among data entities. Conventional graph-structured data can represent pairwise relationships only, whereas hypergraph enables us to associate any number of entities, which is essential in many real-life applications. Hypergraph learning algorithms have been well-studied for numerous problem settings, such as node classification, link prediction, etc. However, much less research has been conducted on anomaly detection from hypergraphs. Anomaly detection identifies events that deviate from the usual pattern and can be applied to hypergraphs to detect unusual higher-order associations. In this work, we propose an end-to-end hypergraph neural network-based model for identifying anomalous associations in a hypergraph. Extensive experimentation on several real-life datasets demonstrates the effectiveness of our model in detecting anomalous hyperedges. **[v1]** Sat, 7 Dec 2024 12:52:22 UTC (11,569 KB). ## Access Paper:. results.title: Hypergraphs and centrality measures identifying key features in gene expression data - ScienceDirect
results.content: ## Mathematical Biosciences. Volume 366, December 2023, 109089. # Original Research Article Hypergraphs and centrality measures identifying key features in gene expression data. Author links open overlay panel, , , ,. Under a Creative Commons license. ## Highlights. Identification of unique behaving genes through hypergraphs. Application of centrality measures to reveal salient features of data. Useful visual tools and representations of hypergraphs and graphs. Discussion of the significance of genes with respect to mathematics and biology. ## Abstract. Multidisciplinary approaches can significantly advance our understanding of complex systems. For instance, gene co-expression networks align prior knowledge of biological systems with studies in graph theory, emphasising pairwise gene to gene interactions. In this paper, we extend these ideas, promoting hypergraphs as an investigative tool for studying multi-way interactions in gene expression data. Additional freedoms are achieved by representing individual genes with hyperedges, and simultaneously testing each gene against many features/vertices. Further gene/hyperedge interactions can be captured and explored using the line graph representations, a technique that reduces the complexity of dense hypergraphs. Such an approach provides access to graph centrality measures, which identifies salient features within a data set. For instance dominant or hub-like hyperedges, leading to key knowledge on gene expression. The validity of this approach is established through the study of gene expression data for the plant species *Senecio lautus* and results will be interpreted within this biological setting. ## Keywords. ## Data availability. Data will be made available on request. ## Cited by (0).

results.title: co.combinatorics - What are the applications of hypergraphs? - MathOverflow
results.content: # What are the applications of hypergraphs? Hypergraphs are like simple graphs, except that instead of having edges that only connect 2 vertices, their edges are sets of any number of vertices. $\begingroup$ A general comment here is that a hypergraph is an absurdly general object; it's basically an element of the power set of the power set of a set. $\begingroup$ Here are two partial explanations for why algorithms based on hypergraphs are less common than algorithms based on graphs. 1. Some polynomial-time algorithms for graphs turn into NP-complete problems when you try to generalize them to hypergraphs (e.g., finding a perfect matching). In this situation there is usually some restriction on the number of vertices a hyperedge can contain and this important class of hypergraphs is no longer absurdly general. Since 3-Sat is one of the most important algorithmic problems in computational complexity theory, hypergraphs play an important role there. $\begingroup$ Hypergraphs (with no uniformity restriction) are also the natural way to model clause sets of general SAT. The reaction network and the underlying hypergraph are related via the stoichiometry matrix, which is a matrix consisting of ones, zeros and minus ones which generalizes the adjacency matrix of a graph. Hypergraphs have been very useful algorithmically for the following "Steiner tree problem:" given a graph (V, E) with a specified "required/terminal" vertex subset R of V and a cost for each edge, find a minimum-cost set of edges which connects all the terminals (and includes whatever subset of V \ R you like). I like this application since one must view the hypergraph as "like a graph" (want it to be connected and acyclic) and not like a set system. "it's a much more complex structure than a regular graph" Hypergraphs could be represented as ordinary graphs, if one represents each "hyperedge" with an additional ordinary node and ordinary edges which connect the new node with the nodes incident to "hyperedge". The Erdős–Rado sunflower lemmas[1], a key discovery of extremal graph/set theory, are about an intrinsic order or emergent "structure" to "random" hypergraphs if certain somewhat modest constraints are satisfied. Inside mathematics, there are many other applications of these hypergraphs in group theory, extremal combinatorics and graph theory.
